title: Time Management Mastery Check
instructions: Verify your understanding of time blindness and time management strategies for ADHD founders.

questions.prompt_markdown: **What is the primary reason ADHD founders experience time blindness?**
options: They don't care about deadlines
They're too busy to track time
Neurological differences in how ADHD brains process temporal information
Poor time management education
questions.explanation_markdown: Time blindness is caused by **neurological differences in how ADHD brains process temporal information**. The internal 'clock' that tracks time passing is unreliable or absent in ADHD brains. It's not a behavioral or educational issue—it's brain wiring.
questions.hint: Think about the biological basis, not behavioral causes.

questions.prompt_markdown: **The 3X Rule suggests multiplying your time estimates by 3 because:**
options: ADHD founders work 3 times slower than others
It accounts for systematic ADHD optimism bias and time estimation blindness
Every task has 3 phases: planning, execution, and review
You should triple-check your work for quality
questions.explanation_markdown: The 3X Rule **accounts for systematic ADHD optimism bias and time estimation blindness**. ADHD brains consistently underestimate task duration—not because they work slowly, but because time perception is inaccurate. The 3X multiplier compensates for this predictable pattern.
questions.hint: It's about perception accuracy, not work speed.

options: Not being able to see far ahead in planning
The ADHD experience of only NOW and NOT NOW, making distant deadlines feel abstract until they become urgent
Working too slowly to meet long-term goals
Difficulty switching between tasks at different time scales
questions.explanation_markdown: Time horizon blindness is **experiencing only NOW and NOT NOW**—a deadline next week and next month both feel like NOT NOW until suddenly they become NOW (urgent). This makes it extremely difficult to start tasks until they reach crisis urgency.
questions.hint: Think about how distant deadlines feel: concrete or abstract?

questions.prompt_markdown: **Visual timers and Pomodoro technique primarily help with:**
options: Working faster
Making invisible time visible during work sessions
Estimating how long future tasks will take
Creating urgency for distant deadlines
questions.explanation_markdown: These tools **make invisible time visible**—they compensate for time perception blindness by providing external awareness of passing time. This is especially helpful during hyperfocus when internal time sense completely disappears.
questions.hint: What do these tools show you in real-time?

questions.prompt_markdown: **Why is tracking actual time spent on tasks valuable for ADHD founders?**
options: To prove you're working hard enough
To build a personal time database that replaces optimistic guessing with evidence-based estimates
To find ways to work faster
To compete with other founders on productivity
questions.explanation_markdown: Time tracking **builds a personal time database** that replaces unreliable intuition with evidence. When you know 'quick emails' actually take 45 minutes on average, you can give accurate estimates instead of optimistic guesses.
questions.hint: It's about using data to improve future estimates.

questions.prompt_markdown: **True or False: The best way to handle time blindness is to practice time awareness until your internal clock improves.**
options: True
False
questions.explanation_markdown: **False!** Time blindness is neurological—you can't 'practice' your way to better time perception. The solution is external systems (timers, tracking, structured scheduling) that compensate for time blindness, not attempting to fix it.
questions.hint: Can you fix neurological differences through practice?
